post.text:
Talk to your @openclaw over a “hacked” Google Home mini! 🦞

I finally updated this project w/ a configurable pipeline you can run entirely locally

Code & getting started in🧵 https://t.co/KEQNjWX5gO

Your same Mac mini can act as a hub for multiple of these around your home.

Stalling & streaming handle OpenClaw’s multi-step agentic responses, so it talks back to you as it works instead of waiting till the end.

You can get PCB’s off PCBWay to retrofit your Google Home Minis

...but to make it easier I also added support for a $13 “Atom Echo” with push-to-talk.

It's fun to carry your Claw around the house, and fire off requests "phone free" https://t.co/rgjYDRiSAL

All code, firmware, PCB files & links in Github. 
 
I hope this inspires more tinkering. And if building ambient HW & natural voice experiences is your type of thing, come join us @Sesame! ✨

https://t.co/UTt0p6B7wx

comments.name: mary davis
comments.text:
This is such a cool way to give an agent a physical voice. Using a Google Home
mini makes it feel like a real assistant in the room. Local pipelines are great
for privacy but the biggest headache is usually keeping the server alive and
handling the network tunnels so the hardware can talk to the model without the
connection dropping

I actually built QuickClaw to solve the infra side of this. It deploys your
instance to the cloud in about 60 seconds so you have an always on backbone for
projects like this. That way your Google Home stays responsive even when your
main computer is off. You can check the link in my bio if you want to move the
backend off localhost :)
